The allow setting lets the agent proceed without interruption.
The ask setting pauses and requests your explicit approval first.
The deny setting blocks the action outright with no prompt and no exception.

The allow outcome means the agent proceeds without interruption.
The ask outcome means the agent pauses and asks for your explicit approval first.
The deny outcome means the action is blocked outright, with no prompt and no exception.
Rules can target specific patterns, such as allowing 'git status', asking for 'git *', and denying 'rm *'.
Permission rules are set in 100xprompt.json.

Every command runs under a timeout.
The default timeout for commands is 2 minutes.
Telling 100xprompt up front that the e2e suite takes about five minutes allows it to set a longer timeout for that command instead of cutting the run short.
When a command is running longer than expected, you can send it to the background rather than cancel it.

The Plan agent is designed to be read-only.
100xprompt has two primary agents that you can drive directly.
Plan is look-but-don't-touch and can read, search, and reason across your whole project to scope work and draft a plan without modifying source files (writing only plan notes).
Build has full read-and-write power to write code, edit files, run commands, and ship real work.
Switching to Plan locks writes for the rest of that turn until you switch back.
In the terminal, pressing Tab cycles to the next agent, and Shift+Tab goes back.
The agent-list shortcut opens the full picker and defaults to Ctrl+X then a.
For non-interactive runs, you can pass the agent by name when kicking off the run (e.g., using --agent).

"How It Works" presents the mental model behind 100xprompt.
When you describe an outcome, 100xprompt reads your codebase, forms a plan, uses real tools to make changes, checks its own work, and asks before doing anything sensitive.
100xprompt works in a core loop consisting of Understand, Plan, Act, Check, and Finish.
During the Understand phase, 100xprompt reads the relevant code before touching anything.
During the Plan phase, it breaks the request into steps, with a visible checklist for larger tasks.
During the Act phase, it edits files, runs commands, and searches code.
During the Check phase, it inspects every result and self-corrects mistakes such as failing tests, typos, and missing imports.
During the Finish phase, it summarizes what changed.
A session is one thread holding the conversation, changes, and the plan so you never re-explain what you're building.
You do not need to know how 100xprompt works to be productive, but it helps you steer it and get better results on short tasks.
